accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum in England Year 5 Earth and space statutory requirements (movement of the Earth relative to the Sun; Earth's rotation explains day and night and the apparent movement of the Sun across the sky), NASA Space Place 'What causes day and night' and 'How long is a year' (rotation about 24 hours noon to noon, about 23 h 56 min against the stars; orbit about 365.25 days, hence leap days), and Royal Museums Greenwich on leap years. The lab turns Earth anticlockwise as seen from above the North Pole, so sunrise is the edge turning into the light and the Sun appears to rise in the east; the adult text notes the sidereal day, the century rule ('most years divisible by 4'), the nearly circular orbit and that the Sun is drawn far too small.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented day-night misconceptions (Vosniadou and Brewer 1994, Mental models of the day/night cycle; Baxter 1989, Children's understanding of familiar astronomical events): the Sun goes round Earth (step 2 prediction, challenge 'round', p5, m9), the Sun goes out or is covered by the Moon (challenge 'out' and 'cover', p1), mixing up spin and orbit so one orbit makes a day or one spin takes a year (step 1 and step 4 predictions, challenge 'year', 'day', m8), day everywhere at once (step 2 prediction, challenge 'all', m2) and Earth going round the Moon ('moon').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagspin is built on Earth's own two motions: a top-down Earth with a lit Sun-facing half that the learner rotates by dragging round it, a clock driven by rotation angle (24 hours per turn), two people on opposite sides, a linked top view and Ava's-eye sky where the Sun's position comes only from Earth's spin, and an orbit path where dragging Earth counts days and spins to 365. flagmoonph drags the Sun along a sky arc and steps Moon phases; flagsky sorts day and night pictures; flagdaylen charts daylight hours by month; flagstar compares star sizes. None rotates Earth. lab_distinct gate passes under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner turns Earth and sees the clock reach 24 hours on one turn; sees Ava go dark while Ben goes light without the Sun moving; spins from 6 am and watches the Sun climb from East and drop at West in Ava's sky while the top view shows only Earth turning; drags Earth round its orbit and watches the day and spin counters both reach 365. The text after each task names the idea the learner has just seen.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'About 365 days' for one spin (the counter shows 24 hours), 'Midday too' for the far side (Ben is in the dark half), 'The Sun goes round Earth' (only Earth turns in the top view), and 'Once' for spins per orbit (the spin counter reaches 365).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with nine distinct feedback messages naming the slip: the Sun going out, the Moon covering the Sun, a year for a spin, an hour for a spin, 24 hours for an orbit, a month for an orbit, the Sun going round Earth, day everywhere at once, and Earth going round the Moon. Answer order rotates between questions.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and everyday words (spins like a top, travels round, the half that faces it), with axis and orbit each explained once in plain words; adult text names the Year 5 statutory wording and the key vocabulary. Canvas labels are one to four words (Ava, East, West, Birthday, Spin: 1 day). validate_lessons readability passes for kid and adult text.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean. Each of the four kid paragraphs carries one idea (the spin about the axis in 24 hours, the day and night halves, the apparent motion of the Sun, the orbit and the year). Items mix reasoning types: explaining night (p1), multiplying spins by 24 hours (p2), naming a year (p3), counting orbits by years (p4, m7), apparent motion (p5, m9), the axis (m1), the far side (m2), counting hours on (m4) and sorting spin from orbit (m8).

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 light and 360 px Android dark screenshots of every step after Show me. On phones the sky step stacks the top view over Ava's sky; East, West and Ava's sky chips sit on the grass band; name labels sit inside the Earth disc so they never cover the Sun or run off the edge; buttons are full-size lbtn (44 px+) in two rows; the orbit fits the canvas with the Birthday chip inside it. Space scenes use fixed dark colours with white chips, so they read the same in both themes.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a labelled button twin: Spin 3 hours, Spin 1 hour and Spin back for rotation; On 1 month, On 1 week and Back to the birthday for the orbit; Spin: 1 day and Orbit: 1 year for the sort. The canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result (Ava's clock time and whether her side faces the Sun, both people's day or night, sunrise and sunset, the day and spin counts on the orbit). walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
